chapters.title: One card, many clues
chapters.subtitle: Read before you memorise.

blocks.title: A nuclear identity
blocks.text: A radionuclide is a radioactive nuclide. Its name pairs an element with a mass number: K-40 is a potassium isotope with 40 nucleons.

blocks.title: One property at a time
blocks.text: Half-life, decay and context offer different clues. You do not need to know everything: compare the same property across cards.

chapters.takeaway: A question links a scientific property to a group of cards.

chapters.title: The nucleus sets the identity
chapters.subtitle: Protons and neutrons, two different roles.

blocks.title: The element
blocks.text: A nucleus contains protons and neutrons. The number of protons identifies the element: hydrogen has one.

blocks.title: Isotopes
blocks.text: H-1 and H-2 are both hydrogen. The second has one extra neutron. Not all isotopes are radioactive: both of these are stable.

chapters.takeaway: Same element does not mean same isotope or half-life.

chapters.title: How a nucleus changes
chapters.subtitle: Five processes to recognise.

blocks.title: Particles and transformations
blocks.text: Alpha emission removes a small group of nucleons. Beta processes and electron capture change the number of protons.

blocks.title: Remember the neutrinos
blocks.text: Neutrinos and antineutrinos are very difficult to detect. β− emits an antineutrino; β+ and electron capture emit a neutrino.

chapters.takeaway: A γ transition releases energy: it does not change the element.

chapters.title: Transformation ≠ radiation
chapters.subtitle: Separate the first process from what you observe.

blocks.title: The decay mode
blocks.text: It describes the nuclear transformation. Observed radiation may also come from later processes, such as daughter-nucleus de-excitation.

blocks.title: The PET example
blocks.text: The β+ branch of F-18 emits a positron and a neutrino. The positron slows, then annihilates with an electron: the roughly 511 keV photons come from this step, not the primary nuclear decay.

chapters.takeaway: Seeing γ photons alone does not identify the decay mode.

chapters.title: Half, then half again
chapters.subtitle: A collective pattern, not an individual timer.

blocks.title: A statistical law
blocks.text: After one half-life, half the undecayed nuclei remain on average; after two, a quarter; after three, an eighth. Under the same conditions, activity follows this reduction too.

blocks.title: Think in time scales
blocks.text: An individual nucleus decays at random. Matter does not disappear: the nucleus changes. Orders of magnitude often suffice to compare cards.

chapters.takeaway: Ask about a half-life interval without memorising every value.

chapters.title: One phenomenon, many contexts
chapters.subtitle: Medicine, nature, environment and beyond.

blocks.title: Origin and use are different
blocks.text: Natural radioactivity concerns radionuclide origin. Environmental monitoring concerns where radionuclides are and how they are measured, including artificial ones.

blocks.title: Context matters
blocks.text: Radioactivity is a physical phenomenon. Usefulness and risk depend on the situation, radionuclide properties and exposure.

chapters.takeaway: A radionuclide can belong to several contexts: categories are not exclusive.
contexts: Nuclei in space and from cosmic rays

chapters.title: Exposed does not mean contaminated
chapters.subtitle: The difference is the presence of radioactive material.

blocks.title: Two distinct situations
blocks.text: Exposure means a person or object receives ionizing radiation. Contamination means radioactive material is present on the surface or inside.

blocks.title: No automatic transfer
blocks.text: Being near a patient after PET does not make another person radioactive. Ordinary exposure does not automatically transfer radioactive material.

blocks.title: Risk depends on context
blocks.text: Activity, radiation type, dose, duration and exposure route matter. Energy alone does not determine risk.

chapters.takeaway: Ask: is radiation arriving, or is radioactive material present?

chapters.title: A good question reshapes the group
chapters.subtitle: Its usefulness depends on the remaining cards.

blocks.title: From broad to specific
blocks.text: Start with application, decay or a half-life interval; then use answers to remove incompatible cards and narrow the search.

blocks.title: The deck decides
blocks.text: A useful question splits the group informatively. The same question may help now and be useless later: watch how the counts change.

chapters.takeaway: In the game, the Learning Engine will help you test these mental models.

chapters.title: Three numbers for a nucleus
chapters.subtitle: Z identifies the element. A and N distinguish isotopes.

blocks.title: Count the nucleons
blocks.text: Z counts protons; A counts all nucleons. The neutron number is N = A − Z.

blocks.title: Same Z, different N
blocks.text: U-235 and U-238 both have 92 protons, but 143 and 146 neutrons respectively. The notation is symbolic: there is no need to draw hundreds of spheres.

chapters.takeaway: Z selects an element; A distinguishes its isotopes.

chapters.title: Follow A. Follow Z.
chapters.subtitle: Each transformation leaves a signature in the nucleus.

blocks.title: Nuclear bookkeeping
blocks.text: Alpha reduces A by 4 and Z by 2. β− raises Z by 1; β+ and electron capture lower it by 1. A stays unchanged in all three weak processes.

blocks.title: Energy and state
blocks.text: A γ transition preserves A and Z: the energy state changes. The p/n sketches alone do not describe the energy balance of a real nucleus.

chapters.takeaway: Check both the nucleon change and the emitted particles.

chapters.title: The particle that balances the books
chapters.subtitle: Weakly interacting does not mean optional.

blocks.title: Simultaneous conservation
blocks.text: Neutrinos and antineutrinos participate in conserving energy, momentum, angular momentum and lepton number. In β decay the available energy is shared among products, including nuclear recoil.

blocks.title: Not the practical card clue
blocks.text: They interact very weakly and are not normally the observable used on the cards. Including them is essential to understanding the process, without adding a new question category.

chapters.takeaway: β− → ν̄e; β+ and EC → νe.

chapters.title: The clock of an ensemble
chapters.subtitle: Half-life and mean lifetime describe the same law.

blocks.title: A constant probability rate
blocks.text: λ is the decay probability per unit time in the infinitesimal-interval limit. In an isolated ensemble N(t) follows exponential decay; A(t) = λN(t).

blocks.title: Two characteristic times
blocks.text: T½ = ln(2)/λ halves the ensemble. τ = 1/λ is the mean lifetime: it is not the half-life. Individual decays remain stochastic.

chapters.takeaway: Compare times and intervals; distinguish mass number A from activity A(t).

chapters.title: From nucleus to detector
chapters.subtitle: A chain of processes, not one label.

blocks.title: Daughter nuclear states
blocks.text: A decay can populate an excited daughter state. Later de-excitation may produce γ or internal-conversion electrons. In electron capture, atomic relaxation may produce X-rays and Auger electrons.

blocks.title: Annihilation after β+
blocks.text: F-18 emits e+ and νe in its β+ branch. After slowing, e+/e− annihilation produces the photons used in PET. The two roughly 511 keV photons are not primary nuclear gamma emissions of F-18.

chapters.takeaway: An observed γ photon alone does not identify the primary mechanism.

chapters.title: Detect. Locate. Treat.
chapters.subtitle: Different physical properties, different goals.

blocks.title: PET and SPECT
blocks.text: PET measures pairs of annihilation photons in coincidence. SPECT uses emitted γ photons and collimation to reconstruct the tracer distribution.

blocks.title: Therapy: where does the energy go?
blocks.text: α particles generally have short range and high linear energy transfer (LET). β− particles generally travel farther with less dense ionization. Radiopharmaceutical distribution also matters.

chapters.takeaway: Application depends on radiation, timing and biological distribution.

chapters.title: Three phenomena to separate
chapters.subtitle: Exposure, contamination, activation.

blocks.title: Exposure and material
blocks.text: Exposure means receiving radiation; contamination means radioactive material is present. Ordinary diagnostic exposure does not automatically make matter radioactive.

blocks.title: Activation is a reaction
blocks.text: Under suitable conditions, reactions induced by appropriate particles or sufficiently energetic photons can produce radioactive nuclei. Projectile type, energy, target nuclide and reaction probability are decisive.

blocks.title: A contextual risk
blocks.text: This is not a common effect of ordinary diagnostics. Risk depends on activity, radiation, energy, dose, duration, distance, intake route and biological distribution, not energy alone.

chapters.takeaway: Identify the physical mechanism before generalising about risk.

chapters.title: A chemical clue, a nuclear property
chapters.subtitle: Two complementary layers of deduction.

blocks.title: The element’s role
blocks.text: Periodic-table family, state at specified conditions and chemical behaviour belong primarily to the element and its electron structure.

blocks.title: The isotope’s role
blocks.text: Half-life and decay depend on the nucleus. Isotopes have similar chemistry, with possible isotope effects: a chemical family does not determine a decay mode.

chapters.takeaway: Use chemistry as a supporting clue alongside nuclear properties.
